name: Bremelanotide

card.summary: PT-141 / Vyleesi, an Rx melanocortin peptide approved for low desire in premenopausal women and bought gray-market by some men; it has no studied role in looks, and pigment spotting is a known side effect.
card.note: Prescription drug in the US; label lists nausea, transient blood pressure rises and focal hyperpigmentation. Gray-market vials are unregulated.

quick.overview:
Bremelanotide (PT-141) is a synthetic peptide related to alpha-MSH, the hormone behind tanning and pigment. It was approved by the US FDA in 2019, under the brand name Vyleesi, for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder [2]. It is a self-administered, on-demand injection [2].

It appears in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding spaces mainly as a libido compound, discussed alongside Melanotan-type tanning peptides, and some men buy it from peptide vendors [12][16]. No trial has tested it as an appearance treatment; its published human research concerns sexual function.
quick.mechanism: Bremelanotide activates several melanocortin receptors. According to the US label, binding to MC1R and MC4R is most relevant at therapeutic dose levels, and the way it improves desire in women is unknown [9]. MC1R sits on pigment cells, which is why pigment changes can occur [9]. Earlier work suggested MC3R and MC4R in the central nervous system are involved in sexual response [5].
quick.risks: In the integrated phase 3 data, nausea (40.0% vs 1.3% on placebo), flushing, headache and injection-site reactions were the most common adverse events, and nausea was the leading reason for stopping [3]. Transient blood pressure increases occur after dosing, and the label advises against use in people at high cardiovascular risk [9]. Focal hyperpigmentation was rare at labelled use but occurred in over a third of subjects after up to 16 consecutive daily doses [3]. Products sold by research-peptide vendors are not regulated as medicines.

lead: Bremelanotide, also known as PT-141 and marketed as Vyleesi, is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) that acts as a melanocortin receptor agonist [2][5]. It was first explored by Palatin Technologies for erectile dysfunction and later developed for women, and the US FDA approved it in June 2019 for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) [1][2][24].

Bremelanotide is not an appearance treatment. It is included in this wiki because it is a close relative of the tanning peptide Melanotan II, is activated at the same pigment-related receptor (MC1R), and is discussed in the same communities, mostly as a libido compound used off-label or sourced from gray-market peptide sellers [9][12][16]. Forum posts describe mixed personal results [14][15].

Published human research is confined to sexual function. Randomized phase 3 trials supported approval in women [2][6], and the safety record from more than 3,500 participants in 43 studies has been reviewed [3]. The label and trial reports document nausea, transient blood pressure elevation, and focal hyperpigmentation as notable effects [3][9].

Its story is tied to the tanning peptides. University of Arizona researchers working on sunless-tanning analogues of alpha-MSH in the 1980s produced Melanotan I and Melanotan II, and bremelanotide is described as a likely metabolite of Melanotan II [24][25]. Melanotan II became a gray-market tanning and libido product that health agencies have warned against since 2007, which is how bremelanotide came to be discussed beside it in tanning, bodybuilding and peptide communities [25][12].

paras: Bremelanotide is not marketed or studied as an appearance treatment. Its link to looks runs through pigment biology and community practice. It acts on the melanocortin system, in which MC1R on pigment cells controls melanin production and tanning, and the label ties focal hyperpigmentation of the face, gums and breasts to this activity [9][26]. Melanotan II, its chemical relative, is the compound people have used for skin darkening, and bremelanotide appears in the same forum threads and vendor catalogues [12][25].

People in these communities also describe libido and confidence as part of looking and presenting well, which is the reason many men ask about PT-141 alongside testosterone therapy and erectile drugs [14][15]. No published trial has examined bremelanotide for skin tone, tanning or any facial outcome.

The US label indicates Vyleesi for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD that causes marked distress and is not due to a co-existing medical or psychiatric condition, relationship problems, or the effects of a medication or drug substance [9]. It is described as an on-demand therapy that the patient administers herself by subcutaneous injection, in contrast to a daily oral drug [2]. The other drug approved for the same indication is flibanserin, and the two are reviewed together in clinical overviews of HSDD [4].

subs.h: Use in men and off-label use
paras: Early development was in men. Reports from around 2003 to 2004 described rapid, dose-dependent increases in erectile activity after PT-141 in healthy men and men with erectile dysfunction, and an intranasal spray was in phase II development for erectile dysfunction [5][6][18]. Pharmacokinetic and safety studies were also carried out with subcutaneous dosing in men, including men who responded inadequately to sildenafil [7]. Bremelanotide is not approved for use in men or for erectile dysfunction [9].

Five melanocortin receptors, MC1R to MC5R, are G protein-coupled receptors. MC1R governs pigmentation and underlies the tanning effect of synthetic alpha-MSH analogues; MC2R is the ACTH receptor; MC3R is linked to growth and lean mass; MC4R is linked to appetite and body weight, and its defects cause a form of obesity; MC3R and MC4R are also implicated in sexual function [26].

Bremelanotide is a non-selective agonist. The US label gives a potency order of MC1R, MC4R, MC3R, MC5R and MC2R and states that how it improves desire is unknown [9]. Wikipedia describes it as acting primarily at MC3R and MC4R in the central nervous system [24]. In rats and non-human primates, PT-141 produced penile erections and activated hypothalamic neurons [5].

Interest began with 1960s studies in which alpha-MSH caused sexual arousal in rats [24]. In the 1980s University of Arizona scientists synthesised alpha-MSH analogues as potential sunless tanning agents, including Melanotan I (now afamelanotide) and Melanotan II [25]. Wikipedia reports that researcher Mac Hadley mistakenly injected twice his intended dose of Melanotan II and had an eight-hour erection with nausea and vomiting, an episode often cited as the origin of the sexual-function research [24].

Melanotan I was licensed to the Australian start-up Epitan, renamed Clinuvel in 2006, and Melanotan II to Palatin Technologies, which stopped developing it in 2000 and developed bremelanotide, a likely metabolite [24][25]. Palatin developed PT-141 as a nasal spray for erectile dysfunction, with a phase IIb trial in men completed in September 2003 [18]. King Pharmaceuticals agreed in 2004 to co-develop the drug in the US, according to Wikipedia, but the FDA halted intranasal phase II trials in 2007 because of blood pressure increases, and Palatin dropped the nasal formulation in 2008 [24]. A dispute with Competitive Technologies over ownership was settled in 2008, with Palatin keeping bremelanotide [24][25].

Development resumed with a subcutaneous autoinjector and women with sexual dysfunction. Two phase 3 trials began at the end of 2014 [20][17][24]. Palatin announced results in November 2016, and in January 2017 AMAG Pharmaceuticals took North American rights [24]. The FDA accepted the application in June 2018 and approved Vyleesi on 21 June 2019 as a first-in-class drug [2][24]. The label names Cosette Pharmaceuticals as the contact for adverse reaction reports [9].

Women. A phase 2 dose-finding randomized trial in premenopausal women with female sexual dysfunction was reported in 2016, and a larger phase 2 registration enrolled 612 women with sexual arousal and/or desire disorders [22][10]. Two replicate randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (known as RECONNECT; each registered with roughly 700 participants) formed the basis of approval, and their results were published in 2019 [20][17][21]. A prespecified and integrated subgroup analysis of those trials was published in 2022 [21]. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of treatments for female desire, arousal and orgasm disorders performed pooled analyses for bremelanotide alongside flibanserin and mindfulness-based therapy [19].

Safety. A 2022 review of the full development programme (43 completed studies, about 3,500 subjects) reported nausea in 40.0% versus 1.3% on placebo, flushing in 20.3% versus 1.3%, headache in 11.3% versus 1.9%, and injection-site reactions in 5.4% versus 0.5% in the integrated double-blind phase 3 data [3]. There were no deaths and few serious adverse events [3].

Men. Early-phase studies in men tested intranasal and subcutaneous PT-141 for erectile response and pharmacokinetics [5][6][7]. No study has examined bremelanotide for facial appearance, skin tone or tanning as an outcome.

Other research. Registered studies have examined bremelanotide with tirzepatide in obesity (phase 2), in diabetic kidney disease (phase 2, 16 participants), the role of MC4R in HSDD (phase 4), and drug concentrations in breast milk [11][20]. Preclinical work in female rats has examined effects on solicitation behaviour [8].

The RECONNECT trials have been analysed critically. In 2021 and 2024, psychologist Glen Spielmans and colleagues published re-analyses arguing that many protocol-listed outcomes went unreported in the original publication, that the efficacy scales have questionable validity for women with HSDD, and that effect sizes ranged from nil to small [27][28]. The 2021 analysis, using the FDA application data, also reported higher study discontinuation due to adverse events on bremelanotide and a preference for placebo as measured by completion and open-label enrolment [28]. Those authors concluded the benefits are statistically modest [27][28].

The trial investigators reported statistically significant improvements in desire and in distress from low desire versus placebo, including across age, weight, BMI and testosterone subgroups in a prespecified 2022 analysis of 1,202 patients [21]. A 2024 expert round-table review noted that flibanserin and bremelanotide are the only approved drugs for HSDD in the US, that none is approved in Europe, and that controversy over pharmacological treatment of young women with HSDD is ongoing [29].

The label lists nausea, flushing, injection-site reactions, headache and vomiting as the most common adverse reactions (incidence above 4%) [9]. Nausea was the most common reason for discontinuing in the clinical programme [3].

Each dose produces a transient rise in blood pressure and fall in heart rate that usually resolves within 12 hours, and the label advises considering cardiovascular risk and says the drug is not recommended in patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease [9]. Ambulatory monitoring in trials showed small, transient but statistically significant blood pressure increases [3].

Focal hyperpigmentation, reported in the label by about 1% of patients at up to 8 doses a month and involving the face, gums and breasts, is more likely in people with darker skin and with daily dosing [9]. In the safety review, it was rare at labelled use but occurred in more than a third of subjects after up to 16 consecutive daily doses [3].
The label notes that the few pregnancies in trials are insufficient to assess risk, and that animal studies at high exposures raise the possibility of fetal harm [9].

Bremelanotide is a cyclic heptapeptide analogue of alpha-MSH [5][7]. The label describes it as a non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist with a potency order of MC1R, MC4R, MC3R, MC5R and MC2R, and states the mechanism by which it improves HSDD is unknown [9]. MC4R is thought to be important in sexual function, and neurons expressing it are widespread in the central nervous system [2][9]. MC1R activation on melanocytes increases melanin expression and pigmentation, which the label links to hyperpigmentation [9]. In rats and non-human primates, PT-141 produced penile erections and activated hypothalamic neurons [5].

Bremelanotide is a cyclic heptapeptide lactam analogue of alpha-MSH with the formula C50H68N14O10 and a molar mass of about 1,025 g/mol, and it differs from Melanotan II in having a carboxyl group where Melanotan II has an amide [24]. After subcutaneous injection, Wikipedia reports about 100% bioavailability, peak levels near one hour, plasma protein binding of 21% and an elimination half-life of about 2.7 hours [24].

Melanotan II is a gray-market peptide used for skin darkening and reported libido effects. Wikipedia lists facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning, appetite loss and erections as reported effects, and darkening of moles and freckles [25]. Whether it affects melanoma risk is unclear: a 2013 review found no conclusive evidence it causes melanoma, and a 2021 review attributed higher risk among users to greater UV exposure [25]. Health agencies began warning against its use in 2007, including the UK MHRA in 2008 and a US FDA warning letter in 2009 [25].

A long-running T Nation information thread on Melanotan I and II lists PT-141 and bremelanotide among the pharmaceutical names of related peptides, reflecting how the compounds are grouped in peptide forums [12].

On T Nation, men on testosterone replacement therapy or struggling with libido or erections have asked about PT-141, with some reporting that PDE5 inhibitors did not help and others describing PT-141 as inconsistent or expensive, to be reserved for special occasions [14][15]. Threads include people who bought vials from peptide sites and asked how to prepare them [16][23][13]. The wiki does not reproduce preparation or dosing instructions.
Press coverage described the approval with the label female Viagra and reported on expert scepticism, according to Wikipedia's reference list, and some commentary questioned its benefit [24].

In the US, Vyleesi is a prescription drug approved for premenopausal women with HSDD, and the label advises against use in people at high cardiovascular risk and not with certain other conditions [9][24]. Wikipedia's account covers only the US approval, and a 2024 review states no HSDD drug is approved in Europe [24][29]. Peptide vendors sell unlicensed bremelanotide as a research product; these are not regulated as medicines.

Related melanocortin compounds include Melanotan II, afamelanotide (Melanotan I, approved by the FDA in 2019 for a rare genetic sun-sensitivity disorder), modimelanotide and setmelanotide, which is approved for rare genetic obesity [24][25][26].

timeline.event: Studies show alpha-MSH causes sexual arousal in rats, prompting interest in melanocortin peptides.[24]
University of Arizona researchers develop Melanotan I and II as sunless-tanning analogues of alpha-MSH.[25]
Palatin stops developing Melanotan II and moves to bremelanotide.[24][25]
Phase IIb trial of intranasal PT-141 in men with erectile dysfunction completed.[18]
King Pharmaceuticals agrees to co-develop PT-141; pharmacokinetic studies in men published.[24][6][7]
FDA halts intranasal phase II trials over blood pressure increases; health agencies begin warning against Melanotan use.[24][25]
Palatin and Competitive Technologies settle ownership dispute; Palatin keeps bremelanotide.[24][25]
Two phase 3 RECONNECT trials in premenopausal women begin with an autoinjector.[20][17][24]
AMAG Pharmaceuticals acquires North American rights from Palatin.[24]
FDA approves Vyleesi on 21 June for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD.[24][2]
Spielmans publishes a re-analysis of the RECONNECT trials questioning outcome reporting.[28]
Prespecified subgroup analyses from RECONNECT and a safety review of 43 studies published.[21][3]
Phase 2 study of bremelanotide with tirzepatide in obesity begins.[11]

lore.intro: In peptide and TRT forums, PT-141 is discussed as a libido and erection aid sourced from research-peptide vendors, and is often mentioned next to Melanotan tanning peptides [12][14][15].

claims.claim: PT-141 can raise libido and help when PDE5 inhibitors fail
claims.believers: Forum users suggest it to men who report low drive or poor response to sildenafil or tadalafil, and some describe it as helpful for libido on TRT [13][14][15].
claims.experts: Early trials in men reported rapid, dose-dependent erectile responses, including in men who had responded inadequately to sildenafil, but the drug was approved only for premenopausal women with HSDD, and no approval exists for men [5][7][9].

claims.claim: Results are "hit and miss" and it is mainly for occasional use
claims.believers: One thread describes its effects as inconsistent, expensive and only suited to special occasions, and another user says it had no effect for them [14][15].
claims.experts: Trials were on-demand designs, and the label describes use as needed with a limit on frequency; the label says the mechanism by which it improves desire is unknown [2][9].

claims.claim: PT-141 belongs to the same family as Melanotan II tanning peptides
claims.believers: Melanotan information threads list PT-141 and bremelanotide as related peptides [12].
claims.experts: Bremelanotide is a melanocortin agonist with MC1R activity, and the label warns of focal hyperpigmentation, particularly with darker skin and daily dosing [3][9].

claims.claim: Vials from peptide sites are a way to use PT-141 without a prescription
claims.believers: Several threads describe users ordering vials from peptide vendors and asking about preparation [16][23].
claims.experts: The approved product is a prescription autoinjector with defined labelled use [9]. No studies assess the contents or safety of gray-market products.

claims.claim: PT-141 is a safer, non-tanning cousin of Melanotan II
claims.believers: Threads group the two as related peptides, with PT-141 chosen for libido rather than tanning [12][14].
claims.experts: Both act at melanocortin receptors including MC1R, and the label warns of focal hyperpigmentation, which can be lasting, with frequent dosing [9][24][25].

claims.claim: PT-141 works through the brain rather than blood flow
claims.believers: Forum users contrast it with PDE5 inhibitors, describing it as a drive or desire compound [14][15].
claims.experts: Preclinical work reports hypothalamic activation and the label says the mechanism for improving desire is unknown [5][9].

claims.claim: The approved drug gives women meaningful gains in desire
claims.believers: The trial investigators report significant improvements in desire and reduced distress versus placebo across subgroups [21].
claims.experts: Spielmans and colleagues argue effect sizes are small to modest and outcome measures weakly validated [27][28].

claims.claim: Nausea and blood pressure effects are mild enough to ignore
claims.believers: Some users report tolerating the compound for occasional use [14].
claims.experts: Nausea occurred in 40.0% versus 1.3% on placebo, and blood pressure rises after each dose; the label advises against use in people at high cardiovascular risk [3][9].

claims.claim: Bremelanotide could help appearance by changing skin colour or body weight
claims.believers: Melanocortin compounds are discussed in tanning and weight-loss circles because MC1R drives pigment and MC4R relates to appetite [26][25].
claims.experts: No trial has tested it for appearance; its weight and obesity effects are in early registered studies with tirzepatide [11][24].
